title: We Ran Our Town's First Night Market (Everything Went Wrong)
creator: Ruth Adeyemi
description:
Six months of planning, forty-two vendors, one thunderstorm.

Thank you to every vendor, volunteer and neighbor who showed up, and to everyone who stayed after to help us pick up soggy cardboard at midnight.

The next night market is planned for May. Vendor applications open in February.

sentences.t: Okay, so I've been teasing this on my stories for months, and it finally happened.
Last Saturday, our little town had its first ever night market.
And I helped organize it, which, if you know me, you know I have never organized anything bigger than a birthday dinner.
So let me tell you how it went, because it was the best and worst day of my year.
It started back in the spring, when my friend Dee and I were at a night market in the city and she said, why don't we have one of these?
And I said, how hard can it be?
Famous last words.
The first thing we learned is that you need a permit for absolutely everything.
A permit to close the street, a permit for food trucks, a permit for amplified music, and insurance on top of all of it.
All in, we needed about six thousand dollars before a single vendor showed up.
And we had about four hundred dollars between us.
So we spent most of the summer going around town looking for sponsors.
Honestly, people were so much more generous than I expected.
Hartley's Hardware sponsored all the string lights, and Mr. Hartley even came out on a ladder to hang them himself.
Calloway Bakery sponsored the little music stage, and the credit union on Elm Street covered the insurance.
In return, we put all their names on a big painted banner at the entrance, which my nephew painted, and it was slightly crooked.
A couple of sponsors didn't even want their name up there, they just said they wanted something fun to happen in town again.
Then we needed vendors.
We were hoping for maybe fifteen, and we ended up with forty-two.
Dumplings, tamales, a lady who makes the most incredible jerk chicken in a converted horse trailer, candles, vintage clothes, a guy selling hot sauce he makes in his garage.
We had a waiting list, which felt insane for a first year.
So, the day itself.
Setup started at two, and by four it was ninety degrees and not a cloud in the sky.
Gates opened at six, and people just kept coming.
By seven thirty, we'd run out of trash bags, two vendors had sold out completely, and the line for dumplings went around the block.
I was running around with a walkie talkie feeling like a festival director.
And then, at about eight fifteen, the sky turned green.
I'm not exaggerating, it went this weird green color, and then it absolutely poured.
Thunder, lightning, the whole thing.
Everyone ran under the awnings, the band unplugged everything, and Dee and I just stood in the middle of the street, soaked, looking at each other.
But here's the part that got me.
Nobody left.
People crammed under every tent, the band started playing acoustic, and the vendors kept serving food in the rain.
When it cleared up around nine, the street was full again, and it was honestly the best part of the night.
We stayed until one in the morning cleaning up, and a bunch of strangers stayed to help us.
So, would I do it again?
Ask me in a month, right now I just want to sleep.
But we're already talking about a spring one, with a lot more tents this time.
If you were there, thank you so much, and tell me what your favorite stall was in the comments.
